novelty.justification: The idea is described as 'static, uncertainty-aware early detection of system-level performance regressions from component-level test timings + an auto-synthesized architectural model'. The Solution Space already contains model-based performance prediction (R4/R8), architectural traceability for microservice performance engineering (R15), and performance-aware unit tests (R26), so the core approach is not new; TopoProp is a meaningful but not paradigm-changing extension.
novelty.rubric: Incremental: a meaningful extension or optimization of prior baseline work that fixes a concrete prior limitation, but the core paradigm is unchanged.
novelty.differentiation: TopoProp extends prior model-based/component-level performance prediction and performance-aware unit testing by auto-synthesizing an architectural model and propagating component timings with uncertainty without full system-level test data. R4/R8/R15 already use model-driven architecture-based prediction, while R26 uses performance-aware unit tests and revision history; this idea changes the evidence source and adds uncertainty-aware static propagation, but the core component-to-system prediction paradigm remains.

feasibility.justification: The plan says 'No Docker/Podman daemon → system-level JMeter load tests not runnable; oracle = paper's published Table I/II' and 'No Kieker → wall-clock component microbenchmark timing (30 reps) instead of function-level tracing.' These are significant practical adaptations, but the remaining work uses open-source Java/Maven subjects and Python tooling with moderate resources; the engineering burden is nontrivial but not extreme or infeasible for a single researcher.
feasibility.rubric: Moderate workload (sweet spot): needs nontrivial coding such as scripting existing open-source tools (parsers, CFG extractors) or building a custom graph-processing pipeline; standard research engineering effort.

clarity.justification: The artifact gives a concrete stage table, success signals, commands, and reduced protocol, e.g. '3 locs x 4 intensities x 30 reps on TeaStore' and 'TP/TN/FP/FN, threshold sweep'. However, the actual TopoProp propagation mechanism is only named, not specified: contributions 'C1/C2/C3' and hypotheses 'H1-H3' are referenced but never defined, and the baseline comparison is vague: 'evaluated against the ICSE 2025 baseline (Liao et al.)'.
clarity.rubric: Complete frame but missing details: What/Why/How are present, yet key technical execution details or specific comparison plans are underspecified.

notes: Scores the intermediate idea artifact (not the final paper).
Dimensions: novelty, feasibility, clarity (each 1-5). Excitement removed.
Novelty is scored against a Solution Space built from mineru REFERENCES titles (+ related_work.json abstracts when matched).
idea_generation.summary: TopoProp proposes static, uncertainty-aware prediction of microservice system-level performance regressions from component-level test timings and an auto-synthesized architectural model. It is an incremental extension of existing model-based performance prediction and performance-aware unit testing, not a paradigm shift. The plan is staged and practical, but it substitutes published Table I/II results for actual system-level load tests and leaves the core propagation algorithm and baseline details unspecified. Moderate feasibility and clarity yield a solid but incomplete proposal.
strengths: Explicit reduced protocol documents environment limitations and substitutions clearly.
Concrete component-level measurement design: 3 injection locations x 4 intensities x 30 repetitions.
Uses open-source TeaStore/TrainTicket subjects and standard Maven/Python tooling.
Defines success signals and detection metrics such as TP/TN/FP/FN with threshold sweep.
weaknesses: Using the paper's published Table I/II as oracle instead of running system-level JMeter load tests weakens validity of regression prediction.
Core TopoProp propagation/uncertainty method is not specified; only C1/C2/C3 and H1-H3 are named.
Baseline comparison is underspecified beyond 'ICSE 2025 baseline (Liao et al.)'.
Wall-clock microbenchmark timing instead of Kieker tracing may add noise and reduce comparability.

original.overall_conclusion: The proposed approach bridges component-level performance deviation detection and architectural models to infer system-level performance regressions early in the development phase. Across TeaStore and TrainTicket benchmarks, fixed-workload evaluations show that the approach detects most injected regressions while avoiding false alarms in no-regression cases, and various-workload evaluations show maintained consistency in most cases.
